title: The Catacombs of Paris
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore the Paris Catacombs, beginning with personal anecdotes about visiting them (and a niece who appeared in the film Mary). They cover the origins of the tunnels in Paris's limestone quarries, the city's sinkholes and overbuilding, the 18th-century cemetery crisis, the Inspection Générale des Carrières (IGC) and chief inspector Charles-Axel Guillaumot, the transfer of bones from cemeteries like the Holy Innocents, the 1786 consecration, and the ossuary wall-building under inspector Louis-Étienne Héricart de Thury. They then discuss other uses of the tunnels (wine and beer storage, mushroom farming, Chartreuse legend, hiding during the Revolution and WWII), the tour details (cost, hours, descent, Ariadne's thread, Porte Mahon replica), off-limits areas and cataphiles (including the Pirates' cinema, the UGC-affiliated Urban Experiment group, and a Chopin concert), the cataflics police and fines, the Opéra Garnier reservoir and Phantom of the Opera, Assassin's Creed Unity, Nadar's 1861 photographs, the Hospital in the Rock in Budapest, crime and bone theft, the ghost Philibert Aspairt, and a viral video. The episode closes with a listener correction about a game show episode concerning syndication and Chuck Barris.

segments.title: Opening and iHeart intro
segments.summary: Show opening and introduction of the Paris Catacombs episode.

segments.title: Opening banter about visiting the catacombs
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the catacombs being like the Moulin Rouge of human bones, share a story of visiting with a niece who appeared in the film Mary, and set up the topic.

segments.title: Origins of the tunnels in Paris quarries
segments.summary: The tunnels began as limestone quarries about two thousand years ago. Paris is built atop roughly 300 km of tunnels, and the old quarries were overtaken by city growth, leading to sinkholes and collapses.

segments.title: Cemetery overcrowding and the IGC
segments.summary: Parisians wanted burial in their home parishes, causing disease concerns. A 1730s study was followed by King Louis XVI creating the Inspection Générale des Carrières in 1777 under chief inspector Charles-Axel Guillaumot, who planned to shore up the mines and move bodies.

segments.title: Moving bones and consecration of the catacombs
segments.summary: Bones were moved at night from Holy Innocents and nearby cemeteries between 1785 and 1787 and deposited in old mine shafts. The site was consecrated in April 1786 and was first called the Paris ossuary before the name catacombs took over.

segments.title: Bone walls, famous burials, and Perrault
segments.summary: In 1810 inspector Louis-Étienne Héricart de Thury arranged bones into walls with skulls facing out. Famous interments include Robespierre and painter Simon Vouet, and the hosts mention Charles Perrault, the figure behind Mother Goose tales.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Alternative uses: brewing, mushroom farming, wartime and revolution hiding
segments.summary: The stable sixty-degree temperature made the tunnels useful for brewing and storing wine and beer and for mushroom farming, with about a thousand tons of mushrooms a year. Revolutionaries and a 1930s group hid there, and buildings had doors to the tunnels until recently; during WWII they were possibly used by Nazis or the Resistance.

segments.title: Tour details: hours, cost, and conditions
segments.summary: The tourist catacombs are open Tuesday to Sunday, roughly 9:30 to 8:30, and cost about 31 euros. The tour is down a long spiral staircase, with electric lights only since the 1970s and sodium lighting; the tour takes about an hour.

segments.title: Porte Mahon corridor and Ariadne's thread
segments.summary: The tour passes a replica of the Porte Mahon fortress carved from memory by an inmate who died during the work, and a black line called Ariadne's thread is painted to prevent visitors getting lost; the hosts discuss its mythological origin.

segments.title: Off-limits catacomb rooms
segments.summary: Many of the most interesting chambers are off-limits to the public and illegal to enter, including the Plage (beach) room with a painted beach scene.

segments.title: Cataphiles, underground art, and parties
segments.summary: The hosts describe a Pirates-style movie theater set up by a group under the Palais de Chaillot, the artist collective UX (Urban Experiment) and its subgroup that restored a clock in the Pantheon, and cataphiles who hold parties and concerts, including a Chopin funeral march performed by a 45-piece orchestra in the 1800s. Punk culture moved underground in the 1970s and 80s.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Cataflics, fines, and property rights below ground
segments.summary: Cataflics, a special gendarmerie detachment, patrol the tunnels; genuine cataphiles are likely left alone while tourists risk a roughly 60 to 65 euro fine. Owners of Paris property reportedly own what lies below it. Cat flaps are reopened entry points into closed areas.

segments.title: Phantom of the Opera and the Opera reservoir
segments.summary: The Phantom of the Opera's underground lake is linked to a real reservoir built under the Paris Opera House to hold water during construction, roughly twelve feet deep and about 60 meters long. The hosts also mention the catacombs appearing in Assassin's Creed Unity.

segments.title: Gaming tangent: Alan Wake 2
segments.summary: Hosts chat about playing horror games, with Chuck describing Alan Wake 2 as scary.

segments.title: Nadar's catacomb photography
segments.summary: Photographer Nadar used battery-operated artificial light to take photographs in the catacombs over three months starting in 1861, with eighteen-minute exposures, so workers in some photos are dummies.

segments.title: Hospital in the Rock, crime, and bone theft
segments.summary: Josh recommends the Hospital in the Rock in Budapest, a cave hospital with mannequins. Thieves stole wine worth over a quarter million dollars from a cave in 2017, and bones have been stolen, sometimes sold to medical students.

segments.title: Ghosts and viral video
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the ghost Philibert Aspairt, a hospital worker who got lost in 1793 and whose voice is said to be heard when candles go out, and a widely circulated, likely fake 2017 video of a man lost in the catacombs.

segments.title: Listener mail: correction on game show syndication
segments.summary: A listener corrects an earlier episode, noting that Chuck Barris did not invent syndication, that earlier syndicated game shows existed, and that syndication grew in 1972 after the FCC returned the 7:30 slot to local stations.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener email and the show closes with iHeartRadio credits.
